prompt: A tall portrait snapshot taken by someone leaning over the brass-and-glass balustrade of the third floor of a huge suburban shopping centre, looking straight down into its central atrium on a busy Saturday afternoon in about 2005. The near edge of the frame is the top rail of that balustrade, caught bright and slightly blown out by the camera's own little flash, a fingerprint smear of glare on the glass panel below it. Beneath, three stacked galleries of shopfronts curve around the void, each one a plain lit window of folded clothes, trainers or homeware under a smooth fascia band painted a single flat colour and left completely blank. At the bottom sits a three-tier marble fountain throwing white plumes into a round pool whose floor glitters with hundreds of copper and silver coins, ringed by big potted palms and slatted wooden benches. A capsule lift with glass walls hangs halfway up its column, a few tiny passengers inside. Further down, a crowded food court of round tables and plastic trays, shoppers as small soft blurs mid-stride with carrier bags swinging, every face too small and smeared to read. Overhead a long barrel-vault skylight pours flat white daylight over everything, bouncing off glossy cream floor tiles and polished chrome. Shot on a cheap early digital compact: slightly soft, a touch of sensor noise in the shadows, highlights that wash out to white, colours a little faded toward warm cream, mint, terracotta and pale blue, horizon a few degrees off level. Every surface is wordless: bare shop fascias, plain carrier bags, unmarked trays and cups. Busy, warm, prosperous, ordinary: the feeling that there was money and somewhere to go. Thanks.
